And at the end she combed it, and she did the part on the wrong side, the way she has done it wrong for thirty-one years, and I never once told her.
I have had four hundred and eleven days and then five hundred and then more to think about which of the two women in this story was good to me.

The answer is both. The answer is that one of them robbed me and asked me first, and the other one loved me and never asked at all, and if you want a clean moral out of that you’re reading the wrong man’s account.
ELEVEN. THE MACHINE
The machine came in January, four days after the anniversary, and it came because of Toya, and Roz never knew that either.

Bev the pathologist had mentioned eye-tracking back in the second month and it went nowhere — the county program had a waitlist and Roz had four hundred other things and the word trajectory had been used, and there is a quiet mathematics in a house like mine where nobody says out loud is it worth it for the time he’s got.

Toya put my name in. Twice. Then called them in December and stayed on hold for fifty minutes in my front room with the phone on speaker so I could hear the hold music, which was a saxophone version of a song I hated in 1988, and she said, “You’re gonna have to sit through this with me, we’re in it together now.”
It’s a monitor on an arm with a camera bar under the screen. You look at a letter and the cursor goes there. You hold a half second and it takes it.
The tech calibrated it in about twenty minutes, and the first thing I typed, on the second of January, with my wife standing on one side of the bed and Toya on the other, was:
THANK YOU
Then, after a minute:
TURN THE TV OFF PERMANENTLY

And they laughed, both of them, and Roz put her face in her hands and laughed until she was crying, and Toya said, “Told you. He’s mean,” and I want to say that was a good afternoon. That was the best afternoon anybody had in that house in two years.
Then everybody went home and I lay in the dark with a machine beside me and did the arithmetic for the last time.
Because I could say anything now.

Fourteen words a minute at first, then twenty. Anything. The whole nine thousand words. I could say: Del was driving. I could say: my wife wrote every one of those pages. I could say: Toya Grant has a codicil.

And I want to walk the reader through it exactly the way I did it that night, because I’ve been accused my whole life of being a cold man and this is the coldest thinking I ever did and I did it with the clearest head I’ve had since January of the year before.
Option one. I tell the truth about 1996.

What happens: Roz finds out that everything she has built since 2004 is wrong. Not slightly wrong. Wrong at the foundation. Twenty years of a marriage she survived by understanding her husband as a coward who fed his brother to the wolves — and the actual explanation is that her husband was just a mean man for no reason at all, which is worse, because a reason is a kind of comfort.

She burns seven weeks of pages. And then she has to sit with the fact that she wrote them. That she conducted a séance with her own dying husband and called it hearing him. That’s not a thing a person recovers from at fifty-two, alone, in a house on Ridgeland with a dead man in it.

And Del. Del reads nothing, and gets nothing, and stays what he’s been since he was nineteen, which is a man who killed a nine-year-old girl and knows it and gets no relief, ever, from anybody, until he dies.
Nobody is saved. That’s option one. The truth costs two people everything and buys nobody a single thing.
Option two. I say nothing and let the pages stand.

Roz keeps her picture. Del gets handed the pages, believes them, and gets — this is the part I turned over for six hours — Del gets to be forgiven. Not by a court. By his brother, in writing, at the end, saying it was mine and I let you carry it. He’ll believe it because it’s in my house in my wife’s hand and because he has wanted it to be true for twenty-nine years without ever once permitting himself to want it.
Del at forty-seven gets to put it down.

And it costs him nothing, because he’ll never know. He’ll go on being a man who thinks he did it and also a man whose brother says he didn’t, and human beings can hold that combination indefinitely — I’ve watched this whole neighborhood do it for thirty years with worse material.
And the price of option two is one thing only: I go into the ground as the man who ran a nine-year-old girl down and let his brother do eleven years for it.
Now. Here’s where I want to be honest, because I’ve read enough about myself in the last two years to know that I don’t get to be the hero of this and I’m not going to try.

Because there’s a version of me that does this for love. There’s a version where Marek Sokol, at the end, in a bed, finally does one decent thing for his brother and his wife and takes the weight, and if you want to read it that way you go ahead, and Bernie Kaczmarek will read it that way and so will the parish and so will everybody at the wake with a plate in their hand.
And there’s another version.

In the other version, I have spent thirty-one years being hated by a woman who never once asked me a question, and I am not going to hand her, at the end, the relief of having been wrong. She built it. Let her keep it. Let her carry a dead child-killer’s cardigan smell around that house for twenty more years and never know that the whole load was one she loaded herself.
That’s revenge. That’s the coldest thing a man has ever done to a woman who nursed him for two years and I could do it with eight words on a screen and everybody would cry at the funeral.
I’ve been in here for four hundred and eleven days, then five hundred, then more, with nothing but time.
And I cannot tell which one I’m doing.

I’ve looked. That’s the thing I want written down, at the end, on the record, in my own words for the first time in two years: I have had more time to examine my own motives than any man alive, no distractions, no work, no drink, nothing to do but this, and I got all the way to the bottom of it and there was nothing at the bottom, there was just a man on Ridgeland Avenue who wanted a particular outcome and could not tell you why.

Maybe there’s no difference. Maybe love and getting even are the same muscle and it’s only the direction that changes, and you don’t get to see the direction from the inside, ever, and everybody who’s ever told you why they did something was guessing same as Roz with the board.

Three weeks went by between the machine arriving and the reading, and I typed about four thousand words in them, and I want to account for what I did with the first real voice I’d had in two years, because it says more about me than the ending does.
I did not use it on 1996. Not once. Not a letter.

I used it on: a list of who owed Sokol & Sons money going back to 2019, with amounts, which took two days and which Roz cried over because she had been paying insurance on equipment for two years and there was eleven thousand dollars sitting in receivables she never knew about.

I used it on: where the deed was, where the spare furnace filters were, which of the two shutoffs under the sink was the hot, the name of the guy at the bank, the combination to the safe, which she had never had.

I used it on: a long thing to Court about the boyfriend, about eight hundred words, which I made her promise not to read to anybody, and which was, I think, the only genuinely kind act of my adult life and took me four hours.
I used it on one joke a day for Toya, which was our arrangement, and which she rated out of ten, and which I never once got above a six on because she is a hard grader.
And I came within about ninety seconds, one night in the middle of January, of telling my wife.

She was sitting where she sits. I had the screen. She was talking about the pages, about how she was nearly finished, about whether to type them up so Del could read them easy, and she said — offhand, not looking at me, doing something with the blanket —
“I keep thinking about your mother. That she went not knowing.”
And I looked at the screen and I had the cursor on the D.
Two more letters and the whole thing comes down. Eleven characters, start to finish. Thirty seconds at the rate I was doing by then.

And I sat there with the cursor on the D for a minute and a half while my wife hummed and folded a blanket at the end of my bed, and then she said, “You want it up or down, hon?” — the bed, she meant the bed — and I looked away from the D to say up, because I was uncomfortable, because I had been on that hip for four hours, because there is always, always, always something closer to the front of the line.
And the moment went. Like they do.

I have thought about whether that was cowardice or whether it was a decision I had already made and was pretending to reconsider. I have had a lot of time. I do not know. I genuinely do not know, and the machine cannot tell me, and neither can anybody else.
So. The last week of January. Everybody in the room.
Roz standing beside the bed with her hand on my arm, reading it out loud, all seven weeks of it, in her steady billing-office voice, forty minutes, front to back.
And at the end she folded her hands on the pages and looked at me and asked me the only question she ever asked me in two years.
“Marek. Is that true?”
And the machine was right there. On its arm. Calibrated. Twenty words a minute. Everything I’ve just told you, available, in about eleven minutes.
And I looked up.
Yes.
CODA. SHE ASKED

Del didn’t say anything for a long time. He sat in the recliner with the pages in his lap and his big spotty drywaller’s hands flat on top of them like they’d blow away, and Roz went and stood at the window, and the furnace came on, and out on Ridgeland somebody was scraping a windshield.
Then he got up and came over and put his forehead down on my chest. Right on my sternum, all his weight, forty-seven years old.
And he said, into my shirt: “You dumb son of a bitch. All this time.”
And I laughed.

Of course I did. Thirty seconds of it, that wet honking noise, with my brother’s head on my chest, and he laughed too, the way he always does, and said, “Yeah, yeah,” and wiped his face on my shoulder and stood up and blew out a breath and said he had to get the van off the street before the plow came.

He came back Sunday. He comes every Sunday. He watches whatever’s on and talks about nothing and something has come out of his shoulders that had been in there since he was nineteen, and I have watched it leave him week by week like water going out of a basement, and I’m not going to apologize to anybody for that.
Roz put the pages in the safe in the basement with the deed and my mother’s rings.
There’s about nine or ten weeks left, at a guess. The lungs are the thing now; they always are. I’ve had two of what the discharge summary calls events and there’ll be a third.
Which brings me to the last thing.

Two weeks ago, in the middle of February, Toya was here on a Thursday night doing the linen. Roz was upstairs asleep. And I’d had the machine six weeks by then and I’d said maybe four thousand words on it, mostly practical, some jokes, one long thing to Del’s daughter Court about her boyfriend that I hope she reads in about ten years.
And Toya came in and sat down in the recliner in the dark and said, “You’re quiet.”
And I typed:
I WANT TO ADD SOMETHING TO THE PAPER
She sat forward. “The codicil?”
YES
“Okay.”
THE HOUSE TOO. AFTER ROZ.
She looked at me for a while.
“Marek,” she said. “Your wife’s fifty-three years old. She could be in that house another thirty years. That’s nothing to me. I’ll be dead.”
I know. I typed that. I know.
“Then what’s it for?”

And that’s the question. That’s the one I’d been waiting eighteen months for somebody to ask me, and here it came at eleven o’clock at night from a woman in scrubs with a bad wheel bearing, and I want to put down exactly what I said, because these are the last words in this account and I typed them at fourteen words a minute with my eyes and they took me two and a half minutes and I have never in fifty-six years said anything so slowly or meant it so completely:
SO THERE’S A DOCUMENT SOMEWHERE THAT SAYS WHAT I ACTUALLY WANTED. ONE. ANYWHERE. IN MY OWN WORDS.
She read it twice.
Then she said: “Why me? You know what I did. You were laying right there.”
And I said:
YOU ASKED.

That’s it. That’s the whole thing. That’s the answer to every question in this book and it took me two years and a stroke and a hundred and thirty thousand dollars of equipment in a yard in Lyons to get it into the world.

She robbed me and she asked me first, and she read my blinks properly for eighteen months, and she never once decided in advance what I meant, and out of every human being who has stood at the end of that bed with a casserole and a card and a good heart, she is the only one who ever found out that there was somebody in here.

My wife is a good woman. She loved me for thirty-one years. She never once in her life asked me a question she didn’t already have the answer to, and she is going to bury a man she made up, and she’ll do it beautifully, and everybody at St. Leonard’s will say what a saint she was to that bastard right to the end.

So the pages will stand. Del gets to put it down. Roz gets to keep her picture. Toya gets the trucks and the list and, eventually, a house on Ridgeland Avenue in a suburb she doesn’t live in, for a mother who won’t live to see it.

There’ll be a wake at Zarzycki’s on Cermak and it will be enormous, because that’s what a block like this does, and because the story going around is a hell of a story: the hard man who couldn’t say a soft word his whole life, who got locked in his own body and finally found a way to say all of it. They love that. It’s got shape. It’s got a moral. There’s not one word of it true and it’s the best thing this neighborhood has had to talk about since 1996.
Bernie Kaczmarek will bring the apricot ones.

Father Nowak will say something at St. Leonard’s about how the Lord takes away a man’s voice to teach him what he should have said with it, and everybody will nod, and I’d give a hundred dollars to be able to laugh at that one out loud, on purpose, in the correct place, instead of at random.
Marisol Reyna will not come. Nobody will remark on it.

And Roz will stand at the door of that funeral home for four hours and shake three hundred hands, and every single one of them will say some version of the same sentence, which is he was lucky to have you, and she’ll say he was a good man at the end, and both of those are true and neither of them is about anybody who ever actually existed.
Here’s my last accounting, and then I’m done.
Things I said out loud, unassisted, in two years: none.

Things I got through the board at twenty-two words an hour that were actually mine and arrived unchanged: I make it about six hundred words. Six hundred, in two years, and most of it PAIN and TURN and COLD.
Things said in my name, in my house, in my wife’s handwriting, over seven weeks, now sitting in a safe in my basement next to the deed and my mother’s rings: about nine thousand.
Fifteen to one against.

That’s the number. That’s the whole book. A man’s account of himself at the end is fifteen parts what other people needed him to be and one part what he actually got out — and I’d bet the trucks that the ratio isn’t much different for people who can talk. You’ve just never had it counted.
And me?
I get the map. I get the drowned state of Illinois, and the Sangamon crack, and the light crossing it left to right for ninety minutes at four in the afternoon.

Somebody will paint that ceiling. That’s the thing I can’t get past, lying here in the last of it, and it’s not even a sad thought, it’s just the true one. Somebody will roll right over Rockford in about a year and a half and never know there was a country up there, and they’ll be right to. It was never up there. It was in here the whole time, like everything else.
One blink for yes.
Ask me something.
